sources.description:
I am an LLM researcher working on optimization and efficient training of neural networks. My current research includes low-rank pretraining, spectral regularization, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and reducing the memory cost of language-model training.

I study how optimization and regularization affect the singular-value spectra and effective rank of weight matrices. I am interested in spectral weight decay, nuclear-norm regularization, proximal methods, and Newton-Schulz approximations. A central question is whether training can make a model easier to compress with low-rank factorization while preserving its quality. Related questions concern generalization and memorization under label noise.

Another research direction is optimization for LoRA and other low-rank parameterizations. Relevant topics include Muon-style matrix updates, optimization of factorized weights, rebalancing, spectral constraints, and convergence analysis. I want to understand both the geometry of these updates and their practical behavior when fine-tuning language models.

I also work on memory-efficient LLM pretraining. Relevant methods include low-rank gradient and optimizer-state representations, GaLore, Frugal-style methods, and low-precision optimizer states such as FP8. I am interested in their tradeoffs between model quality, training memory, throughput, and communication cost, including how those tradeoffs change with model scale.

As a secondary current interest, I am building an AI research digest agent with a handwritten harness. Relevant work includes explicit context management, structured LLM decisions, application-controlled tools, and paper retrieval and relevance ranking using lexical or embedding-based methods.

I have not specified hard topic exclusions for this digest.

passages.text: Modern transformers pair impressive capabilities with substantial memory and compute demands. Low-rank weight factorization reduces both while keeping the matrices dense, and thus efficient on standard hardware. Existing methods, however, choose the subspace to remove from each weight matrix with local closed-form criteria: activation energy, layer-wise reconstruction error, or a quadratic approximation of the loss. These criteria ignore how errors propagate through the network, so at high compression the errors compound with depth and performance collapses. We introduce Learnable Subspace Projections (LSP), which instead learns the subspaces to discard end-to-end. Each linear layer, or tied group of layers that read the same activations, is assigned an orthogonal projector. All projectors are optimized jointly against a global objective—the KL divergence to the dense model’s output distribution or the model’s original training loss—while the pretrained weights remain frozen. Projectors are initialized from a whitened SVD truncation, and ranks are allocated by the output KL each projector induces per parameter saved. After training, the projectors merge into standard low-rank factors, with each tied group sharing one factor. In attention, this also lets the model cache one narrow latent in place of full keys and values. Across LLMs (OPT-125M/1.3B, Qwen3-4B, Llama-2-7B) and ViT-B/16, LSP outperforms baselines, and its advantage widens as compression increases. We propose Learnable Subspace Projections (LSP), which does exactly this: every projector is learned against a global objective, by default the KL divergence to the dense model’s output distribution, or alternatively the model’s original training objective, a variant we denote LSP T . Our contributions are: (1) Learned subspace projections. Layers that read the same activations (Q/K/V, gate/up) form a tied group and share one projector; we optimize all projectors jointly across the network with the pretrained weights frozen. An activation-space parameterization with fused QR orthonormalization keeps this tractable at billion-parameter scale. (2) Whitened initialization and measured-KL allocation. Each projector is initialized from a whitened truncation, recast as an orthogonal projector and extended to tied groups. To decide how many directions each layer or tied group removes, we apply each projector in isolation, measure the KL divergence it induces on the model output, and allocate the budget by KL cost per saved parameter. The model at initialization, which we call NoLSP, serves as a control that isolates the effect of learning. (3) Efficient low-rank inference. After training, the projectors merge into plain low-rank factors, so the deployed model contains no LSP-specific operations. At the same compression ratio it requires the same FLOPs per token as other factorizations, yet the input factor shared by each tied group speeds up small-batch decoding and, in a latent-cache deployment, stores one narrow latent per group where untied factorizations store two (one each for keys and values), shrinking the KV cache. LSP outperforms pruning and SVD baselines by a margin that grows with the compression ratio, and on ViT it degrades least among the compared methods when calibration and evaluation distributions differ.

Baselines. All baselines are using the same calibration budget of 1024 1024 sequences of 2048 2048 tokens, run with bf16 weights and compression arithmetic in fp32 or fp64 (following LSP), and, for the SVD methods, are evaluated in factorized form. Where a baseline exposes a tuning knob we sweep it around the published value and keep the best per model and ratio: SVD-LLM’s recovery learning rate against its single published one, Dobi-SVD’s γ \gamma learning rate around the released default, Swift-SVD’s allocation α \alpha over its own eleven-point grid, and ASVD’s α \alpha . Dobi-SVD is run without its quantization step so that parameter counts match; Swift-SVD’s OPT rows are bias-corrected; SVD-LLM’s recovery stage is LoRA of rank 8 8 on the calibration corpus of the table it appears in. Notice that LSP keeps original weights frozen, and learns to compress their subspace, which means it does not move from the original subspace but only projects. SVD-LLM-v2 ( Wang et al., 2025c ) and MoDeGPT ( Lin et al., 2025 ) , though relevant, could not be reported as no official implementation has been released. The ViT ports of SVD-LLM (W) and SliceGPT are adapted from the official released implementation, while FLAR-SVD and PELA come from their official implementation. PELA, specifically, re-trains all the network’s weights with the objective to copy the dense model’s intermediate features, which acts as a recovery fine-tuning stage. Evaluation. Perplexity follows the SparseGPT and SliceGPT convention: the test split is joined, tokenized once and cut into non-overlapping 2048 2048 -token windows. Zero-shot accuracy is measured with the EleutherAI harness ( Gao et al., 2024a ) at zero shots on the merged model, and we report plain accuracy.

Benchmarks. The choice of benchmarks follows other compression methods in the literature. In Table 1 we report perplexity for a diverse mix of pruning and low-rank compression methods, as reported by Ashkboos et al. (2024) ; van der Ouderaa et al. (2024) ; Wang et al. (2025d) ; Wang et al. (2025b) ; Qi et al. (2026) . For zero-shot performance ( Table 2 ) we restrict the analysis to low-rank compression methods ( Wang et al., 2025d ; Wang et al., 2025b ; Qi et al., 2026 ) , since they are the closest to LSP. Specifically, we report the same six benchmark evaluations as baselines do, and calibrate on the same datasets. While Alpaca-calibrated compression follows our compression ratios reported for other tables, for C4-calibrated compression we follow same procedure as Swift-SVD, with compression ratios of − 20 % / 40 % / 60 % -20\%/40\%/60\% , to introduce further richness in compression ratios. We re-evaluate all methods and benchmarks for evaluation fairness, using the same setup for calibration and evaluation for all methods.

passages.text: Recent successes of matrix- and curvature-based optimizers have renewed interest in how update geometry shapes learning. These methods normalize or precondition updates, changing how different components progress during training. In deep matrix factorization, the geometry that slows gradient descent (GD) favors low-rank solutions by delaying the emergence of small singular modes. This raises the question of what remains of that spectral bias when normalization or curvature correction weakens or removes the slowdown. We study how optimizer geometry and depth jointly govern this behavior through a common framework for singular mode dynamics. Under explicit balance and alignment assumptions, we derive birth, saturation, and decay laws for Euclidean GD, coordinate-wise updates of SignGD and an instantaneous Adam approximation, spectral updates of Muon and cumulative Shampoo, and a block curvature model of K-FAC. The resulting picture is not a simple ordering from stronger to weaker low-rank bias. To highlight, SignGD and ideal Muon eliminate the divergent birth barrier and drive unsupported modes to zero in finite time. Cumulative Shampoo initially retains GD’s depth-dependent barrier, then accumulated gradients produce a catch-up phase while making previously active modes increasingly persistent. Undamped K-FAC cancels the factorization-induced slowdown while preserving the ordering of the target singular values, whereas positive damping introduces a spectral threshold below which the slow GD phase laws reappear. These results give normalization, accumulated state, damping, and depth a direct interpretation as controls determining when modes emerge, persist, and disappear during training.

GD and SignGD dynamics establish contrasting reference behaviors. Instantaneous Adam identifies how a positive stabilizer restores slow dynamics at small gradient magnitudes. Ideal Muon accelerates both emergence and removal of modes in finite time. For cumulative Shampoo, an exact accumulator identity quantifies the transition from initialization dominated to history dominated dynamics. For the specified K-FAC block model, an exact birth time decomposition separates an undamped contribution from a damping-weighted GD contribution. Together, these results identify when optimizer geometry preserves, modifies, or cancels the suppression of small modes induced by depth. ( 𝟑 ) \mathbf{(3)} Numerical validation of phase laws and regime transitions. Controlled experiments in deep matrix factorization and regression verify the derived phase laws. These experiments demonstrate that settings commonly associated with numerical stability can change relative spectral progress, determining which components emerge, persist, and disappear during training.

Analyses of gradient flow and gradient descent connect spectral dynamics to low rank recovery and incremental rank growth under specified initialization and measurement assumptions ( Gunasekar et al., 2017 ; Arora et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2021 ; Jin et al., 2023 ) . While depth strengthens the tendency of low rank bias, it is not always equivalent to minimizing a single Schatten norm, indicating that trajectory-level geometry is essential ( Razin and Cohen, 2020 ) . Recent Muon analyses characterize how polar normalization changes spectral learning and simplicity bias in deep linear networks and linear attention ( Dragutinović and Ranganath, 2026 ) , and establish approximately uniform singular value growth under assumptions on LoRA factorization ( Kang et al., 2026 ) . For fully observed bilinear matrix factorization, Rhee et al. (2026) derive uniform factor singular value growth after alignment, and analyze oscillations caused by finite optimization steps. Complementary empirical comparisons show that Muon’s relative performance depends on the factorization problem and hyperparameter tuning ( Parviz et al., 2026 ) . Shampoo has been interpreted as an adapted version of spectral descent that retains information about stochasticity and the parameter trajectory ( Eschenhagen et al., 2026 ) . Building on these results, we compare mode birth, decay, and saturation within a common balanced aligned model. While most analyses study one optimizer in isolation, our analysis includes SignGD and simplified Adam, derives an exact accumulator identity for cumulative Shampoo, and quantifies the effect of additive damping in K-FAC. We give a broader discussion on related works in App. A .

Our analysis shows that the spectral bias of depth depends on optimizer geometry and the stage of training. A surprising consequence is that rapid learning of weak components can coexist with rapid removal of unsupported ones, as illustrated by the Muon analysis. Conversely, accumulated history can accelerate the emergence of a mode while prolonging its persistence. These effects make a single ordering of optimizers by stronger or weaker low-rank bias inadequate. A further implication is that parameters associated with numerical stability also shape learning bias. In the analyzed models, Adam’s stabilizer, Shampoo’s accumulator initialization, and K-FAC’s damping determine where normalization, history, or curvature correction governs spectral progress. They can therefore change how strongly depth suppresses small modes, even within the same optimizer. Although the phase laws rely on balance and alignment assumptions, they identify concrete mechanisms to understand optimizer behavior. This perspective motivates evaluating optimizers through which components they accelerate, suppress, or preserve alongside the training loss, since comparable fit can conceal differences in their dynamics. The resulting framework provides a basis for understanding and testing how faster optimizers change the complexity of intermediate models.

Fig. 4 provides a broader validation of the theory in addition to the theoretical evaluation done in Sec. 6 . Fig. 5 compares the optimization and rank dynamics. Although the methods eventually reach similar losses and effective ranks, their trajectories differ substantially. GD learns the target modes sequentially and retains a low effective rank for longer, consistent with the small mode mobility factor σ p \sigma^{p} . Adam reduces this separation and activates weaker modes much earlier. Muon produces an even more rapid redistribution of spectral mass, reflecting its normalized spectral update. Cumulative Shampoo initially behaves more like GD but quickly changes regime as its accumulated preconditioner adapts. K-FAC exhibits a smoother evolution in which curvature correction reduces the factorization induced separation between mode time scales. The stable and effective rank curves therefore mainly differ during the transient phase, while their later agreement reflects the unique full observation target rather than identical optimization dynamics. All optimizers train the same depth L = 4 L=4 deep linear factorization toward the same rank eight target and reach comparable final training loss. Left: training loss over optimization steps. Middle: stable rank of W W . Right: effective rank of W W . The optimizers exhibit markedly different transient rank dynamics despite converging toward similar final spectra. GD retains a lower rank representation for longer, whereas Adam, Muon, cumulative Shampoo, and K-FAC alter the rate at which spectral mass is distributed across modes.

The singular value trajectories in Fig. 6 make these differences more explicit. Under GD, larger target modes emerge first and weaker modes remain close to initialization for substantially longer times. This sequential emergence is the dynamical mechanism underlying its transient low rank bias. Adam substantially compresses these mode dependent delays, while Muon causes the positive modes to follow nearly the same spectral clock until they encounter their different target amplitudes. Cumulative Shampoo exhibits the predicted two stage behavior: early growth remains separated across modes, after which accumulated gradient history accelerates the weaker modes and reduces target amplitude dependence. K-FAC produces the weakest separation between mode trajectories, consistent with curvature correction compensating for the factorization induced mobility barrier. These trajectories illustrate that optimizers reaching similar final solutions can nevertheless pass through very different spectral representations during training. (a) GD (b) Adam (c) Muon (d) Shampoo (e) K-FAC Figure 6: Singular mode trajectories reveal optimizer dependent spectral clocks. GD exhibits strongly sequential learning;Adam reduces these delays, while Muon makes the modes evolve on nearly the same clock until they approach their respective targets. Cumulative Shampoo shows a faster history adapted growth of weaker modes. K-FAC further reduces the factorization induced separation between mode time scales through curvature correction. The common final amplitudes are determined by the unique full observation target, whereas the transient trajectories expose the distinct inductive biases of the optimizers.

We introduce Clean , a memory-efficient and full-curvature optimizer designed to resolve this bottleneck. Clean leverages the randomized Nyström method to accurately approximate the left and right preconditioners in SOAP, and to reduce the optimizer’s memory complexity from quadratic to linear in terms of model dimensions. We subsequently reintegrate the off-subspace components to capture curvature information beyond the low-rank approximation, preserving rich curvature at minimal memory cost. We further propose Q-Clean , a low-precision variant that aggressively compresses optimizer states. Q-Clean reduces optimizer memory consumption by over 50% compared to Muon when pre-training a LLaMA-1.3B architecture, all while maintaining strong and competitive predictive performance. Notably, Clean operates with a smaller optimizer-state footprint than standard AdamW while reaching AdamW’s final performance 26% faster in wall-clock time. Furthermore, our methods uniquely enable the pre-training of a 13B-parameter model on a single 80GB GPU, providing a scalable, efficient, and accessible approach to large-scale model optimization. $*$ $*$ footnotetext: Equal contribution.

passages.text: We propose a novel optimizer for low-rank adaptation (LoRA) that explicitly incorporates the gauge symmetry of low-rank factorization. Our optimizer extends recent matrix optimizers for full-parameter training to the manifold of fixed-rank matrices by interpreting them as normalization under a rotated basis. We show how rotation and normalization can be integrated with the fixed-rank manifold efficiently. Our optimizer converges faster to lower held-out loss and achieves better or comparable downstream performance on both supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning tasks.

Large language models (LLMs) based on the transformer architecture ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) have achieved remarkable success in recent years ( Brown et al., 2020 ; Touvron et al., 2023 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) . These models typically adopt a pretraining-finetuning paradigm, where large-scale pretraining equips a model with general capabilities and subsequent finetuning adapts it to specific downstream applications. However, as LLMs grow to billions of parameters, full-parameter finetuning becomes expensive in both computation and memory. Such a challenge has motivated the development of parameter-efficient finetuning (PEFT) methods ( Houlsby et al., 2019 ) , which only update a small fraction of all parameters. Among these approaches, low-rank adaptation (LoRA) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) has emerged as a particularly effective method and has been widely adopted. LoRA freezes the pretrained weights and parametrizes the weight updates as products of low-rank matrices, substantially reducing the number of trainable parameters and the memory footprint, while maintaining competitive performance. Compared with full-parameter training, LoRA exhibits a unique geometric structure induced by its low-rank factorization. Specifically, the low-rank matrices have infinitely many reparameterizations that represent the same weight update, since the model’s output depends on these low-rank factors only through their product. This invariance, commonly referred to as gauge symmetry, suggests that optimization should respect the underlying geometry of the weight space of the LoRA parametrization. Motivated by this observation, we revisit the optimization of LoRA and aim to explicitly incorporate its gauge symmetry into the design of the optimization algorithm.

We design our optimizer on the manifold of fixed-rank matrices, aiming to optimize the product of the low-rank factors directly rather than each factor separately. We extend the recent advances in matrix optimizers ( Gong et al., 2026 ; Jordan et al., 2024 ; Vyas et al., 2025 ) to the fixed-rank manifold by interpreting their update rules as normalization under a rotated basis. Our optimizer applies row and column normalization in a conditioning frame defined by the left singular vectors of the tangent momentum, projects the resulting direction back onto the tangent space, and retracts to the fixed-rank manifold. By exploiting the low-rank structure of tangent vectors, all operations can be performed using thin factors without materializing full weight-sized matrices. We refer to our proposed optimizer as RoM ( Ro tated M anifold Optimization). We evaluate RoM on supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning tasks. RoM achieves substantially lower held-out loss and better or comparable downstream task performance compared with other LoRA optimizers, with only modest additional computational overhead.

We evaluate RoM on supervised finetuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) tasks, comparing its optimization and downstream performance against existing LoRA optimizers. We describe the experimental setup in Section 4.1 , present the SFT and RL results in Section 4.2 and 4.3 , respectively, and further study the contribution of its components and its sensitivity to learning-rate selection in Section 4.4 . Large Language Models (LLMs) have become highly effective for natural language understanding and generation; however, their reliance on static parametric memory makes them prone to hallucinations, outdated information, and unsupported factual claims, particularly in scientific and technical domains [9], [10]. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), introduced by Lewis et al. [12], addresses this limitation by coupling language models with external retrieval systems that provide dynamically retrieved evidence during generation. In a standard RAG pipeline, user queries are embedded into vector representations, relevant documents are retrieved from a vector store, and the retrieved context is incorporated into the model prompt for response generation. Although conceptually simple, the effectiveness of RAG systems heavily depends on retrieval quality, ranking strategies, query formulation, and context selection mechanisms [5, 7]. Recent work has proposed multiple enhancements to traditional retrieval pipelines, including query rewriting [14], hypothetical document generation [6], reranking approaches [16], reciprocal rank fusion methods [3], self-reflective retrieval systems such as Self-RAG [1], and agentic retrieval frameworks [15], [18], [19]. While these approaches improve retrieval quality and grounding, they also introduce additional computational cost and architectural complexity. Despite rapid progress in Retrieval-Augmented Generation research, practitioners still lack clear guidance regarding which retrieval strategies perform best under realistic deployment settings and large-scale scientific corpora. Existing studies often evaluate isolated retrieval components or rely on small benchmark datasets that may not reflect real-world scientific search environments.

This paper addresses these limitations by constructing a unified evaluation framework for comparing retrieval pipelines in scientific question answering systems. We evaluate six retrieval strategies: classic dense retrieval, LLM-based query rephrasing, query rephrasing with reranking, multi-query fusion using Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), agentic retrieval, and late-interaction retrieval with ColBERTv2. All pipelines share a common corpus, generator model, and evaluation setup, and the five single-vector pipelines share a common embedding model and vector database, to ensure fair comparison. The contributions of this work are summarized as follows: 1. We construct a unified RAG evaluation framework over a large-scale corpus of scientific literature. 2. We compare six retrieval pipeline strategies under controlled experimental settings. 3. We release a synthetic scientific question-answering dataset generated from arXiv papers across multiple domains. 4. We analyze retrieval quality and response generation using LLM-as-a-judge evaluation methodologies and retrieval-oriented metrics. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work on RAG systems and retrieval optimization techniques. Section 3 presents the methodology and retrieval pipelines, together with the datasets and evaluation setup. Section 4 reports experimental results and analysis. Section 5 discusses the findings, Section 6 outlines limitations, followed by conclusions in Section 7.

Evaluating RAG systems remains challenging because traditional lexical overlap metrics such as BLEU and ROUGE do not adequately capture factual grounding, faithfulness, or retrieval relevance. Jiang et al. found LLMs fail to recognize the personal preferences of user profiles across time [21]. Recent work introduced LLM-as-a-judge methodologies capable of approximating human preference evaluation for open-ended tasks [20]. RAG-specific evaluation frameworks such as RAGAS further extended evaluation toward faithfulness, answer relevance, and contextual grounding [4]. These evaluation methods have become increasingly important for assessing retrieval quality and generation reliability in large-scale RAG systems. Despite rapid progress in RAG research, limited work systematically compares multiple retrieval pipeline strategies under controlled conditions using large-scale scientific corpora. Existing studies often evaluate isolated retrieval components or focus on small benchmark datasets. Our work addresses this gap by benchmarking dense retrieval, query rewriting, reranking, rank fusion, agentic retrieval, and late-interaction retrieval approaches within a unified evaluation framework for scientific question answering systems.

This work presented a systematic, unified evaluation of retrieval strategies for scientific question answering. By benchmarking six distinct retrieval pipelines — ranging from classic dense retrieval to agentic tool-call architectures and late-interaction retrieval — over a corpus of 2024–2025 arXiv papers, we demonstrated that retrieval architecture dominates pipeline complexity: ColBERT’s late-interaction retrieval achieves both the highest gold-paper retrieval rates and the highest answer quality, while among single-vector pipelines Rephrased & Reranked RAG yields the highest answer quality and the simpler Classic baseline provides robust, cost-effective performance.

For each strategy we report results separately for the problem and method query subsets. We report (i) the answer rate — the percentage of queries with is_answer = true — and (ii) the mean of each 1–5 metric. By convention, zero-valued scores are excluded from the metric means, so per-metric averages reflect quality conditional on the model attempting an answer , while the answer rate captures how often it attempts one. We additionally report unconditional means, in which refusals remain as zeros, providing a single end-to-end score over all queries. All six strategies were run on the same 9,742 papers for which query generation succeeded, so each strategy has 19,484 question instances and every cross-strategy comparison is paired at the query level. Because every synthetic query has a known gold source paper, we also compute retrieval metrics directly from the run files: Hit@1 and Hit@3 measure whether the gold paper appears at those cutoffs, and MRR@3 rewards higher gold-paper rank.

Because every synthetic query has a known gold source paper, we can measure retrieval quality directly, independent of the judge. Table 5 reports gold-paper Hit@1, Hit@3, and MRR@3 per strategy and query type. ColBERT retrieves the gold paper within the top 3 for 92.8% of problem queries and 94.8% of method queries — roughly double the best single-vector pipeline (Rephrased & Reranked: 47.5% and 52.8%). The experimental results highlight the critical role of retrieval strategy selection in RAG pipelines. We observed that pipeline complexity does not linearly scale with retrieval performance. Among the single-vector strategies, the “Rephrased & Reranked RAG” approach achieved the highest overall scores (3.77/5), suggesting that model-based re-ranking effectively mitigates retrieval noise, while multi-query fusion and the agentic tool-call pipeline fell below the classic single-shot baseline (3.60/5) despite their additional LLM calls. This indicates that simpler architectures may offer cost-efficiency without significantly compromising performance. The clearest result, however, is the effect of the retrieval architecture itself. ColBERT’s late-interaction retrieval, indexed over the same full 463,971-paper corpus as the Chroma-based strategies, retrieved the gold paper in the top 3 for 92.8–94.8% of queries — roughly double the best single-vector pipeline — and produced the best answers on nearly every quality dimension (overall 3.94/5, paired delta + 0.37 +0.37 vs. Classic). Retrieval quality is linked to index composition, and comparisons of retriever architectures are unreliable unless all retrievers operate over the same document pool. The gold-hit analysis makes the mechanism explicit: conditional on retrieving the gold paper, all strategies produce answers of similar quality (overall ≈ \approx 3.8–4.0), so nearly all of the between-strategy differences are attributable to how often the right evidence reaches the generator, not to how the generator uses it.

passages.text: Double descent has sparked considerable interest, with recent work relating it to the data, the model and the learning configuration. Practical fine-tuning commonly involves training a small adapter on top of frozen pretrained weights, as in low-rank adaptation (LoRA). The adapter’s rank is the hyperparameter that sets its capacity, yet how this rank relates to double descent has not been well explored. We quantify this relation under label noise on four vision backbones and a 7 7 B language model with a module-matched rank sweep (MMRS), which extends past full rank and compares every rank with dense fine-tuning of the same modules, paired by seed. On DeiT-Tiny, risk is lowest at rank one and rises sharply as the adapter becomes able to fit the noisy labels, forming an interpolation cliff. What numerical experiments test the predicted low-rank bias beyond aligned matrix factorization, especially on neural networks or language models, and what limitations do the authors state?

passages.text: Recent successes of matrix- and curvature-based optimizers have renewed interest in how update geometry shapes learning. These methods normalize or precondition updates, changing how different components progress during training. In deep matrix factorization, the geometry that slows gradient descent (GD) favors low-rank solutions by delaying the emergence of small singular modes. This raises the question of what remains of that spectral bias when normalization or curvature correction weakens or removes the slowdown. We study how optimizer geometry and depth jointly govern this behavior through a common framework for singular mode dynamics. Under explicit balance and alignment assumptions, we derive birth, saturation, and decay laws for Euclidean GD, coordinate-wise updates of SignGD and an instantaneous Adam approximation, spectral updates of Muon and cumulative Shampoo, and a block curvature model of K-FAC. The resulting picture is not a simple ordering from stronger to weaker low-rank bias. To highlight, SignGD and ideal Muon eliminate the divergent birth barrier and drive unsupported modes to zero in finite time. Cumulative Shampoo initially retains GD’s depth-dependent barrier, then accumulated gradients produce a catch-up phase while making previously active modes increasingly persistent. Undamped K-FAC cancels the factorization-induced slowdown while preserving the ordering of the target singular values, whereas positive damping introduces a spectral threshold below which the slow GD phase laws reappear. These results give normalization, accumulated state, damping, and depth a direct interpretation as controls determining when modes emerge, persist, and disappear during training.

( 𝟐 ) \mathbf{(2)} Phase laws revealing how optimizer settings shape the bias of depth. We derive birth, saturation, and decay laws that distinguish normalization, accumulated history, and damping. GD and SignGD dynamics establish contrasting reference behaviors. Instantaneous Adam identifies how a positive stabilizer restores slow dynamics at small gradient magnitudes. Ideal Muon accelerates both emergence and removal of modes in finite time. For cumulative Shampoo, an exact accumulator identity quantifies the transition from initialization dominated to history dominated dynamics. For the specified K-FAC block model, an exact birth time decomposition separates an undamped contribution from a damping-weighted GD contribution. Together, these results identify when optimizer geometry preserves, modifies, or cancels the suppression of small modes induced by depth. ( 𝟑 ) \mathbf{(3)} Numerical validation of phase laws and regime transitions. Controlled experiments in deep matrix factorization and regression verify the derived phase laws. These experiments demonstrate that settings commonly associated with numerical stability can change relative spectral progress, determining which components emerge, persist, and disappear during training.

Analyses of gradient flow and gradient descent connect spectral dynamics to low rank recovery and incremental rank growth under specified initialization and measurement assumptions ( Gunasekar et al., 2017 ; Arora et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2021 ; Jin et al., 2023 ) . While depth strengthens the tendency of low rank bias, it is not always equivalent to minimizing a single Schatten norm, indicating that trajectory-level geometry is essential ( Razin and Cohen, 2020 ) . Recent Muon analyses characterize how polar normalization changes spectral learning and simplicity bias in deep linear networks and linear attention ( Dragutinović and Ranganath, 2026 ) , and establish approximately uniform singular value growth under assumptions on LoRA factorization ( Kang et al., 2026 ) . For fully observed bilinear matrix factorization, Rhee et al. (2026) derive uniform factor singular value growth after alignment, and analyze oscillations caused by finite optimization steps. Complementary empirical comparisons show that Muon’s relative performance depends on the factorization problem and hyperparameter tuning ( Parviz et al., 2026 ) . Shampoo has been interpreted as an adapted version of spectral descent that retains information about stochasticity and the parameter trajectory ( Eschenhagen et al., 2026 ) . Building on these results, we compare mode birth, decay, and saturation within a common balanced aligned model. While most analyses study one optimizer in isolation, our analysis includes SignGD and simplified Adam, derives an exact accumulator identity for cumulative Shampoo, and quantifies the effect of additive damping in K-FAC. We give a broader discussion on related works in App. A .

Our analysis shows that the spectral bias of depth depends on optimizer geometry and the stage of training. A surprising consequence is that rapid learning of weak components can coexist with rapid removal of unsupported ones, as illustrated by the Muon analysis. Conversely, accumulated history can accelerate the emergence of a mode while prolonging its persistence. These effects make a single ordering of optimizers by stronger or weaker low-rank bias inadequate. A further implication is that parameters associated with numerical stability also shape learning bias. In the analyzed models, Adam’s stabilizer, Shampoo’s accumulator initialization, and K-FAC’s damping determine where normalization, history, or curvature correction governs spectral progress. They can therefore change how strongly depth suppresses small modes, even within the same optimizer. Although the phase laws rely on balance and alignment assumptions, they identify concrete mechanisms to understand optimizer behavior. This perspective motivates evaluating optimizers through which components they accelerate, suppress, or preserve alongside the training loss, since comparable fit can conceal differences in their dynamics. The resulting framework provides a basis for understanding and testing how faster optimizers change the complexity of intermediate models.

Fig. 4 provides a broader validation of the theory in addition to the theoretical evaluation done in Sec. 6 . Fig. 5 compares the optimization and rank dynamics. Although the methods eventually reach similar losses and effective ranks, their trajectories differ substantially. GD learns the target modes sequentially and retains a low effective rank for longer, consistent with the small mode mobility factor σ p \sigma^{p} . Adam reduces this separation and activates weaker modes much earlier. Muon produces an even more rapid redistribution of spectral mass, reflecting its normalized spectral update. Cumulative Shampoo initially behaves more like GD but quickly changes regime as its accumulated preconditioner adapts. K-FAC exhibits a smoother evolution in which curvature correction reduces the factorization induced separation between mode time scales. The stable and effective rank curves therefore mainly differ during the transient phase, while their later agreement reflects the unique full observation target rather than identical optimization dynamics. Middle: stable rank of W W . Right: effective rank of W W . The optimizers exhibit markedly different transient rank dynamics despite converging toward similar final spectra. The singular value trajectories in Fig. 6 make these differences more explicit. Under GD, larger target modes emerge first and weaker modes remain close to initialization for substantially longer times. This sequential emergence is the dynamical mechanism underlying its transient low rank bias. Adam substantially compresses these mode dependent delays, while Muon causes the positive modes to follow nearly the same spectral clock until they encounter their different target amplitudes. Cumulative Shampoo exhibits the predicted two stage behavior: early growth remains separated across modes, after which accumulated gradient history accelerates the weaker modes and reduces target amplitude dependence. K-FAC produces the weakest separation between mode trajectories, consistent with curvature correction compensating for the factorization induced mobility barrier. These trajectories illustrate that optimizers reaching similar final solutions can nevertheless pass through very different spectral representations during training. Cumulative Shampoo shows a faster history adapted growth of weaker modes. K-FAC further reduces the factorization induced separation between mode time scales through curvature correction. The common final amplitudes are determined by the unique full observation target, whereas the transient trajectories expose the distinct inductive biases of the optimizers.

passages.text: Training large language models (LLMs) entails a fundamental trade-off: memory-efficient optimizers such as Adam discard cross-parameter curvature, whereas full-curvature methods such as SOAP can accelerate convergence at prohibitive memory costs. We introduce Clean , a memory-efficient and full-curvature optimizer designed to resolve this bottleneck. Clean leverages the randomized Nyström method to accurately approximate the left and right preconditioners in SOAP, and to reduce the optimizer’s memory complexity from quadratic to linear in terms of model dimensions. We subsequently reintegrate the off-subspace components to capture curvature information beyond the low-rank approximation, preserving rich curvature at minimal memory cost. We further propose Q-Clean , a low-precision variant that aggressively compresses optimizer states. Q-Clean reduces optimizer memory consumption by over 50% compared to Muon when pre-training a LLaMA-1.3B architecture, all while maintaining strong and competitive predictive performance. Notably, Clean operates with a smaller optimizer-state footprint than standard AdamW while reaching AdamW’s final performance 26% faster in wall-clock time. Furthermore, our methods uniquely enable the pre-training of a 13B-parameter model on a single 80GB GPU, providing a scalable, efficient, and accessible approach to large-scale model optimization. $*$ $*$ footnotetext: Equal contribution.

We compare against AdamW ( Kingma and Ba, 2014 ) , SOAP ( Vyas et al., 2024 ) , Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) , and ALSO ( Romashov et al., 2026 ) . Due to the prohibitive cost of a full sweep at 1.3B, we performed a shortened sweep and resumed only the best configurations to 5,000 steps. Our optimizer extends recent matrix optimizers for full-parameter training to the manifold of fixed-rank matrices by interpreting them as normalization under a rotated basis. We show how rotation and normalization can be integrated with the fixed-rank manifold efficiently. Our optimizer converges faster to lower held-out loss and achieves better or comparable downstream performance on both supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning tasks.

Large language models (LLMs) based on the transformer architecture ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) have achieved remarkable success in recent years ( Brown et al., 2020 ; Touvron et al., 2023 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) . These models typically adopt a pretraining-finetuning paradigm, where large-scale pretraining equips a model with general capabilities and subsequent finetuning adapts it to specific downstream applications. However, as LLMs grow to billions of parameters, full-parameter finetuning becomes expensive in both computation and memory. Such a challenge has motivated the development of parameter-efficient finetuning (PEFT) methods ( Houlsby et al., 2019 ) , which only update a small fraction of all parameters. Among these approaches, low-rank adaptation (LoRA) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) has emerged as a particularly effective method and has been widely adopted. LoRA freezes the pretrained weights and parametrizes the weight updates as products of low-rank matrices, substantially reducing the number of trainable parameters and the memory footprint, while maintaining competitive performance. Compared with full-parameter training, LoRA exhibits a unique geometric structure induced by its low-rank factorization. Specifically, the low-rank matrices have infinitely many reparameterizations that represent the same weight update, since the model’s output depends on these low-rank factors only through their product. This invariance, commonly referred to as gauge symmetry, suggests that optimization should respect the underlying geometry of the weight space of the LoRA parametrization. Motivated by this observation, we revisit the optimization of LoRA and aim to explicitly incorporate its gauge symmetry into the design of the optimization algorithm.

We design our optimizer on the manifold of fixed-rank matrices, aiming to optimize the product of the low-rank factors directly rather than each factor separately. We extend the recent advances in matrix optimizers ( Gong et al., 2026 ; Jordan et al., 2024 ; Vyas et al., 2025 ) to the fixed-rank manifold by interpreting their update rules as normalization under a rotated basis. Our optimizer applies row and column normalization in a conditioning frame defined by the left singular vectors of the tangent momentum, projects the resulting direction back onto the tangent space, and retracts to the fixed-rank manifold. By exploiting the low-rank structure of tangent vectors, all operations can be performed using thin factors without materializing full weight-sized matrices. We refer to our proposed optimizer as RoM ( Ro tated M anifold Optimization). We evaluate RoM on supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning tasks. RoM achieves substantially lower held-out loss and better or comparable downstream task performance compared with other LoRA optimizers, with only modest additional computational overhead.

Large Language Models (LLMs) have become highly effective for natural language understanding and generation; however, their reliance on static parametric memory makes them prone to hallucinations, outdated information, and unsupported factual claims, particularly in scientific and technical domains [9], [10]. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), introduced by Lewis et al. [12], addresses this limitation by coupling language models with external retrieval systems that provide dynamically retrieved evidence during generation. In a standard RAG pipeline, user queries are embedded into vector representations, relevant documents are retrieved from a vector store, and the retrieved context is incorporated into the model prompt for response generation. Although conceptually simple, the effectiveness of RAG systems heavily depends on retrieval quality, ranking strategies, query formulation, and context selection mechanisms [5, 7]. Recent work has proposed multiple enhancements to traditional retrieval pipelines, including query rewriting [14], hypothetical document generation [6], reranking approaches [16], reciprocal rank fusion methods [3], self-reflective retrieval systems such as Self-RAG [1], and agentic retrieval frameworks [15], [18], [19]. While these approaches improve retrieval quality and grounding, they also introduce additional computational cost and architectural complexity. Despite rapid progress in Retrieval-Augmented Generation research, practitioners still lack clear guidance regarding which retrieval strategies perform best under realistic deployment settings and large-scale scientific corpora. Existing studies often evaluate isolated retrieval components or rely on small benchmark datasets that may not reflect real-world scientific search environments.

This paper addresses these limitations by constructing a unified evaluation framework for comparing retrieval pipelines in scientific question answering systems. We evaluate six retrieval strategies: classic dense retrieval, LLM-based query rephrasing, query rephrasing with reranking, multi-query fusion using Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), agentic retrieval, and late-interaction retrieval with ColBERTv2. All pipelines share a common corpus, generator model, and evaluation setup, and the five single-vector pipelines share a common embedding model and vector database, to ensure fair comparison. We identify adaptation imbalance : a few singular directions dominate the trained update, leaving its performance sensitive to how gains are allocated. We argue that learning where to adapt does not ensure that adaptation gains are well balanced . This motivates LoRA-Norm , a post-training normalization method that retains learned directions while rebalancing their gains. LoRA-Norm combines spectral rebalancing, a fixed nonlinear transformation of singular values, with nuclear-norm restoration, which preserves the original total spectral mass. However, freezing pretrained parameters does not preserve pretrained behavior: the added update can improve the target task while compromising capabilities outside the adaptation distribution ( Shuttleworth et al., 2024 ) . This creates a practical challenge for deployment, where specialization and capability retention both matter ( Biderman et al., 2024 ) . An important question is whether a completed adapter can better satisfy these objectives through changes to how its learned directions are used. We examine this question by separating an adapter’s directions from their gains, building on a broader line of parameter-efficient methods that exploit weight decomposition or directional structure ( Meng et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Lingam et al., 2024 ) . Although LoRA constrains the update rank, it does not require adaptation strength to be distributed evenly across these directions. Our measurements reveal substantial concentration in trained adapters, with directional output energy dominated by a small subset of the available components. We describe this uneven allocation as adaptation imbalance and investigate its deployment consequences by changing gains while keeping the learned directions fixed.

Our central argument is that learning where to adapt does not ensure that adaptation gains are well balanced . Training jointly determines directions and gains through a source-task objective, but the resulting configuration can remain improvable for specialization and broader capability retention. Prior work establishes the feasibility of post-training refinement through weight interpolation ( Wortsman et al., 2022 ) , spectral pruning ( Kumaravelu et al., 2026 ) , and calibration-gradient-guided reweighting ( Tian et al., 2026 ) . We investigate a simpler intervention: a fixed normalization rule that revisits the gains of a completed adapter using only its parameters. Figure 1: Learn the directions, normalize the gains. LoRA training learns useful adaptation directions, but the gains assigned to these directions can become imbalanced. LoRA-Norm keeps the learned directions fixed and rebalances only their gains after training, improving specialization while preserving capabilities beyond the target task. We propose LoRA-Norm , which combines spectral rebalancing with nuclear-norm restoration , as shown in Fig. 1 . Spectral rebalancing applies a short, fixed sequence of nonlinear transformations to the singular values while preserving their associated directions. Nuclear-norm restoration rescales the transformed gains to preserve their original sum within each module. This changes the allocation of spectral mass without requiring an exactly flat spectrum. The edited update is reconstructed as standard low-rank factors with the original adapter configuration and scaling. LoRA-Norm therefore requires no calibration data or additional training and introduces no inference overhead.

We evaluate 18 trained adapters spanning two backbones and three adaptation tasks in coding, mathematical reasoning, and instruction following. LoRA-Norm improves average target-task performance and capability retention, exceeding the evaluated spectral-pruning and gradient-guided editing configurations on both measures. These results show that the same learned directions can support better deployment performance after gain normalization, without any additional training. Our analysis also clarifies what this improvement means. Preserving nuclear norm does not preserve update magnitude, and a direction’s functional contribution depends on both its gain and the inputs that activate it ( Paischer et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2024 ) . Controls matched to LoRA-Norm’s activation-weighted update energy recover much of its benefit, while stronger functional equalization provides no consistent additional gains. Thus, balancing adapter gains and equalizing their responses are distinct objectives . Directional concentration is useful for characterizing an adapter, but uniformity alone is insufficient to judge whether an edit improves specialization and retention. We characterize adaptation imbalance in trained LoRA adapters and show that their learned directions can support improved specialization and capability retention through post-training gain adjustment. • Practical method. We introduce LoRA-Norm, a fixed spectral normalization procedure that preserves learned directions and per-module nuclear mass, requiring neither calibration data nor additional training or inference operations.

• Functional analysis. We examine gain redistribution alongside update strength through matched-strength controls and activation-aware interventions, showing why stronger response equalization is not a reliable objective for adapter refinement.
